title: MODULE 07 — Caching, Asynchronous Processing and Messaging

blocks.text: Modern backend applications must handle large amounts of data, respond quickly to user requests and perform operations that should not block the main application workflow.
Imagine PrepSpaces has thousands of students accessing courses, watching lessons, enrolling in programs and using AI-powered interview features.
Thousands of students request the same course information.
A student enrols in a course and the backend needs to send a confirmation email.
An AI interview evaluation takes 30 seconds to complete.
A student updates their profile, but cached information still displays the old details.
An email service becomes temporarily unavailable.
A notification message is delivered twice.
A large number of background jobs need to run without affecting API performance.
Multiple backend instances need to process messages reliably.
Performing every operation synchronously inside an HTTP request can make applications slow and difficult to scale.
This is where caching, asynchronous processing and messaging become important.

In this module, you will learn how to improve application performance using Redis, move time-consuming operations into background workers, communicate through message brokers, implement event-driven architecture and build reliable background processing systems.
The module primarily uses Java, Spring Boot, Redis, RabbitMQ, PostgreSQL and Spring AMQP. Kafka will also be introduced for event-streaming architectures.
By completing this module, you should be able to:
Understand synchronous and asynchronous application execution.
Execute background jobs without blocking API requests.
Understand message queues and message brokers.
Use Redis for caching and shared application data.
Understand cache-aside, write-through and other caching strategies.
Maintain consistency between PostgreSQL and Redis.
Implement retry queues and dead-letter queues.
Build APIs that remain responsive while processing long-running operations.
One of the first decisions in backend engineering is determining whether an operation should execute immediately as part of a request or continue independently in the background.
These approaches are called synchronous and asynchronous processing.
Synchronous processing means the calling operation waits for the requested work to finish before continuing.
Imagine a student requests course enrolment.
If the email service takes 10 seconds, the entire request may remain open while waiting for it.
The user experiences a slow response even though the actual enrolment may have completed much earlier.
Asynchronous processing allows the backend to initiate work and continue without waiting for all the work to finish.
The application can complete the enrolment and delegate email delivery to a background worker.
The main API request does not need to wait for the email operation.
Student | v Enrolment API | v Save enrolment in database | v Publish notification task | v Return successful response Background Worker | v Process notification | v Send confirmation email
Can return before background work finishes
Check whether a user is authorised.
Validate a payment request before initiating it.
Suppose an API starts a background report-generation task.
Instead of waiting for the entire report, the backend may return:

HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted Content-Type: application/json
{ "jobId": "job-1001", "status": "QUEUED", "message": "Your report is being generated" }
The client can check the job status through another endpoint.
Remember that 202 Accepted means processing has been accepted, not that the operation has already completed.
F. Important distinction: Asynchronous vs parallel processing
Asynchronous and parallel processing are related but different.
Asynchronous processing: The caller does not need to wait for the operation to finish.
Parallel processing: Multiple operations execute simultaneously, generally using multiple execution resources.
An asynchronous task may execute later on a single worker. Parallelism is not guaranteed.
Why this lesson matters: You must understand which operations need immediate results and which can run independently before designing a scalable backend.
Lesson 2 — Background Jobs and Task Scheduling
Many backend operations do not need to be executed immediately when a user sends an API request.
Some operations need to run in the background or at a predefined time.
A. What is a background job?
A background job is an operation performed independently of the main request-response workflow.
For example, PrepSpaces might need to:
These operations can be executed by background workers.
A worker is a process or execution component responsible for performing tasks.
Backend API | v Create Background Job | v Job Queue | v Background Worker | v Execute Job | v Update Job Status
The worker can operate independently of the API request.
C. Implementing asynchronous execution in Spring Boot
Spring Boot supports asynchronous method execution using @Async.

@Service public class NotificationService { @Async public CompletableFuture<Void> sendEmail( String email, String message) { // Perform email delivery return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null); } }
Another application component can invoke the method without waiting for its complete execution.
However, @Async is not a complete distributed job-processing solution.
It generally runs inside the same application process and requires appropriate executor configuration.
A thread pool manages a collection of reusable threads.
Instead of creating a new thread every time a job is submitted, the application can reuse threads from the pool.

@Configuration @EnableAsync public class AsyncConfig { @Bean("taskExecutor") public Executor taskExecutor() { ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor(); executor.setCorePoolSize(5); executor.setMaxPoolSize(10); executor.setQueueCapacity(100); executor.setThreadNamePrefix("background-"); executor.initialize(); return executor; } }
These values are illustrative. Production values should be selected according to workload, available resources and downstream service limits.
Task scheduling means running a task at a predefined time or interval.
Every night at midnight, delete expired temporary records.
Every morning, generate learning activity summaries.
Every hour, check pending notification jobs.
Every week, prepare course analytics reports.
Spring Boot supports scheduled execution through @Scheduled.
@Component public class ReportScheduler { @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *") public void generateDailyReports() { System.out.println( "Generating daily reports" ); } }
This example runs at 2 AM according to the configured scheduler timezone.
Wait 10 seconds after the previous execution completes
Run once at a specified time
An important problem appears when your backend runs on multiple instances.
Imagine three backend servers all execute the same scheduled task:
Backend A → Generate report Backend B → Generate report Backend C → Generate report
The same job might execute three times.
For production scheduling, consider whether the job should run once globally or independently on every instance.
Why this lesson matters: Background execution and scheduling allow applications to perform expensive or recurring operations without unnecessarily slowing down user-facing APIs.
Lesson 3 — Message Queues and Message Brokers
Asynchronous processing becomes more powerful when different application components can communicate without directly depending on one another.
Message queues and message brokers make this possible.
A. What is a message queue?
A message queue is a mechanism for storing messages until consumers are ready to process them.
Suppose a student enrols in a PrepSpaces course.
Instead of executing everything inside the enrolment request, the application can publish messages for background processing.
B. What is a message broker?
A message broker is software responsible for receiving, routing, storing and delivering messages between producers and consumers.
A message broker commonly used for task queues, routing, acknowledgements and background processing.
Well suited to the notification-processing lab.
A distributed event-streaming platform designed for durable event streams, high-throughput processing and multiple independent consumers.
Useful for event-driven systems and analytics pipelines.
An in-memory data platform frequently used for caching, counters, coordination and messaging through Streams and Pub/Sub.
Used primarily for caching in this module's practical lab.
C. How a message queue works
Queue: Holds messages waiting to be delivered or processed.
Exchange: In RabbitMQ, routes published messages to queues based on routing rules.
Routing Key: Helps determine where a message should be delivered.
Acknowledgement (ACK): Indicates that a consumer has successfully processed a message.
Negative Acknowledgement (NACK): Indicates that processing was unsuccessful and the message should be rejected or handled according to the configured policy.
Prefetch: Controls how many unacknowledged messages a consumer can receive at a time.
Persistence: Helps messages survive broker restarts when the appropriate durable queues, persistent messages and storage configuration are used.
Depends on queue and broker configuration
These technologies overlap in some use cases, but they have different operating models.
A critical principle is that successful message delivery does not automatically guarantee exactly-once business execution.
Why this lesson matters: Message brokers allow backend components to communicate reliably without requiring every operation to execute inside a single HTTP request.
As backend applications grow, different components need to react to events without being tightly coupled to one another.
Event-driven architecture provides a way to build these systems.
An event represents something that has already happened in an application.
UserRegistered CourseCreated StudentEnrolled PaymentCompleted LessonCompleted InterviewSubmitted CertificateGenerated
An event describes a completed fact, rather than simply requesting that another component perform an operation.
Imagine a student enrols in a course.
Different consumers can react to the same event.
Recommendation service updates relevant activity data.
The enrolment service does not need to directly call all these components.
An event and a command are not the same.
Command: Requests that something should happen.
Event: Announces that something has already happened.
Commands are generally directed to a particular handler. Events can be consumed by multiple interested components.
E. Event-driven architecture vs traditional request-response
Caller may wait for downstream services
Errors can affect the request workflow
Background failures can be managed separately
Since consumers process events independently, different parts of the application may not be updated at exactly the same moment.
Analytics updates a few seconds later.
Notification arrives after another few seconds.
You will learn when eventual consistency is acceptable and when an operation requires an immediate authoritative database response.
Why this lesson matters: Event-driven architecture helps backend systems grow without making every service directly dependent on every other service.
Producer and consumer patterns are the foundation of messaging-based backend systems.
A producer generates messages, while a consumer receives and processes them.
A producer is a component that creates and publishes messages.
For example, when a student completes a course, the backend may publish:
The producer should focus on creating the correct message rather than implementing all downstream operations itself.
A consumer listens to a queue or stream and processes incoming messages.
C. Implementing a producer with Spring AMQP
Assume RabbitMQ is configured and the application has a suitable exchange and routing configuration.

@Service public class NotificationPublisher { private final RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate; public NotificationPublisher( RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate) { this.rabbitTemplate = rabbitTemplate; } public void publishEnrollmentEvent( EnrollmentEvent event) { rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend( "notification.exchange", "notification.enrollment", event ); } }
This sends a message to the configured RabbitMQ exchange using its routing key.

@Component public class NotificationConsumer { @RabbitListener( queues = "enrollment.notifications" ) public void processNotification( EnrollmentEvent event) { System.out.println( "Processing notification for user: " + event.userId() ); // Send email or create notification } }
The consumer runs separately from the request-handling controller.
The actual production implementation must define acknowledgement, retry, dead-letter and idempotency policies rather than assuming every invocation succeeds exactly once.
Suppose a queue contains 1,000 notification messages.
You can run several consumer instances:
Notification Queue / | \ / | \ v v v Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3
Workers can process different messages concurrently.
This increases processing capacity when the downstream service can support the additional load.
Increasing the number of consumers does not always improve performance. For example, if your email provider allows only a limited sending rate, too many workers can trigger rate limiting.
A producer and consumer need an agreed message structure.
You should avoid coupling consumers directly to the entire database entity structure.
Why this lesson matters: Producer and consumer separation allows different backend components to process work independently and scale according to demand.
Redis is an in-memory data platform frequently used to improve application performance.
Instead of retrieving the same information from a relational database for every request, your backend can temporarily store frequently accessed data in Redis.
Redis supports several data structures and operations, including:
It is commonly used for caching, shared counters, session storage, distributed coordination and real-time data.
Imagine 5,000 students repeatedly request the same course information.
5,000 Requests | v Backend API | v PostgreSQL | v Retrieve course data
The database may repeatedly execute identical queries.
5,000 Requests | v Backend API | v Redis Cache | +---- Cache Hit → Return data | +---- Cache Miss | v PostgreSQL | v Save in Redis | v Return data
Repeated requests can be served from the cache.
Redis uses simple commands to manipulate data.
Returns the remaining time to live.
HSET user:101 name Rahul email rahul@example.com HGET user:101 name
One major advantage of Redis is the ability to assign expiration times to stored keys.
This reduces the need to store every cached item permanently.
Although Redis is often described as an in-memory database, it supports persistence options.
You will learn the basics of:
RDB: Creates point-in-time snapshots of Redis data.
AOF: Records write operations so they can be replayed during recovery.
The appropriate persistence configuration depends on whether Redis is being used for disposable cache data or important application state.
For ordinary caching, losing the cache should not mean losing the authoritative application data.
Redis is not a universal replacement for PostgreSQL.
Why this lesson matters: Redis can significantly reduce database load and response time when frequently accessed data is cached appropriately.
Lesson 7 — Cache-Aside and Other Caching Strategies
Caching is not simply storing frequently used information in Redis.
You must decide how cached information is populated, updated and maintained.
Different caching strategies solve different problems.
Caching means storing a copy of frequently required information in a faster storage layer so that future requests can retrieve it more quickly.
For example, a course page may be requested thousands of times without any change to the underlying course information.
Rather than executing the same database query repeatedly, the backend can reuse the cached result.
Cache-aside is one of the most commonly used caching strategies.
The application checks the cache first.
If the information is not available, it retrieves the data from the database and stores it in the cache.
If the key exists, return cached data.
If the key does not exist, query PostgreSQL.
In read-through caching, the application requests data through a caching layer.
The caching component is responsible for loading missing information from the underlying data source.
This places more responsibility on the cache abstraction.
Write-through caching updates the cache as part of the write operation.
Application | v Caching Layer | +---- Update Cache | +---- Update Database
The goal is to keep the cache updated whenever data changes.
However, the implementation must carefully handle partial failures between the cache and database.
Write-behind caching stores updates in the cache first and writes them to the underlying database later.
This can reduce database write pressure, but it introduces additional risks.
For example, if pending writes are lost before reaching the database, important data could disappear.
This is more appropriate for carefully designed workloads where delayed persistence is acceptable.
It should not be used casually for critical enrolments, payments or account operations.
Refresh-ahead caching refreshes frequently accessed data before it expires.
This can reduce cache misses for popular resources.
For example, the backend may refresh frequently requested course catalogues before their expiration time.
Application updates database and manages cache
H. Implementing Redis caching in Spring Boot

@Service public class CourseService { private final CourseRepository repository; public CourseService(CourseRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; } @Cacheable( cacheNames = "courses", key = "#courseId" ) public CourseResponse getCourse(Long courseId) { return repository.findById(courseId) .map(CourseResponse::from) .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException( "Course not found" ) ); } }
The caching abstraction checks the configured cache before invoking the method and stores the result according to its configuration.
For an application using Redis, configure a Redis-backed cache manager.
Why this lesson matters: Different caching strategies allow you to optimise read and write performance according to the behaviour of your application.
Caching creates a new problem: cached information can become outdated.
Imagine an instructor updates a course title.
PostgreSQL contains the new title, but Redis still stores the old version.
This is called a cache consistency or cache invalidation problem.
Cache invalidation means removing or updating cached data when the authoritative data changes.
Old course title: Java Fundamentals New course title: Advanced Java Development
If the cache contains the old title, the backend must ensure that subsequent requests do not continue returning it indefinitely.
It determines how long a cached key remains valid.
The cache entry expires after five minutes.
TTL is simple and useful, but a five-minute expiration does not guarantee that every request receives fresh data.
A value may become outdated immediately after it is cached.
Redis reaches its configured memory limit.
An eviction policy selects the key.
Rejects writes that require additional memory
Evicts least recently used keys with expiration
Evicts keys with the shortest remaining TTL
You will learn why eviction policies should be selected according to the application's cache workload.
E. Cache invalidation after database updates
Suppose an instructor updates a course.
The service should update PostgreSQL and invalidate the corresponding cached value.
@CacheEvict( cacheNames = "courses", key = "#courseId" ) public void updateCourse( Long courseId, CourseRequest request) { // Validate and update database record }
The exact ordering of the cache operation and database commit requires attention.
For reliable behaviour, cache eviction should occur after a successful database transaction commit, or through another appropriate consistency mechanism.
Imagine a popular course's cache entry expires.
Thousands of students request the same course simultaneously.
All requests discover a cache miss and query PostgreSQL.
This creates a sudden database workload increase.
This is called a cache stampede or cache thundering herd.
You will learn strategies such as:
G. Cache penetration and hot keys
Cache Penetration: Requests repeatedly query information that does not exist in the cache or database.
Hot Key: One key receives an unusually large number of requests.
You will learn how negative caching, request validation, caching policy and traffic distribution can help.
Why this lesson matters: A poorly managed cache can return incorrect information or create even more load than the database operations it was designed to reduce.
PostgreSQL and Redis serve different purposes.
PostgreSQL is generally the authoritative store for application records, while Redis frequently stores temporary copies for faster retrieval.
Keeping these systems consistent is an important backend engineering responsibility.
Imagine a student's course progress is 60%.
If the backend reads the cache, it returns 40% even though the actual database value is 60%.
This happens when a database update does not properly invalidate or update the cached information.
The application now has stale cached data.
You need an explicit recovery strategy.
Update PostgreSQL | v Transaction commits | v Invalidate Redis key | v Next request reloads from PostgreSQL
If invalidation fails, you may need retry mechanisms, TTL limits or event-based cache invalidation.
Suppose the backend writes to PostgreSQL and Redis independently.
Write PostgreSQL → Success Write Redis → Failure
The two stores no longer agree.
This is commonly called the dual-write problem.
You will understand why a successful database transaction does not automatically guarantee a successful cache update.
A backend can publish a data-change event after a successful database update.
A cache invalidation consumer removes the corresponding Redis key.
This allows several backend instances to receive the same update and invalidate their relevant cached information.
Reads observe the latest committed state under the system's consistency guarantees
Replicas or dependent stores converge over time
A user sees their own successful updates
Old cached data may be returned while fresh data is loaded
Not every data item should use the same caching strategy.
Carefully controlled caching or authoritative read
Cache only with an explicit write and invalidation strategy
Avoid treating Redis as the final source of truth for critical financial or enrolment operations without a specifically designed persistence and consistency model.
Why this lesson matters: Performance improvements must not introduce incorrect user information or inconsistent business records.
Lesson 10 — Retry Queues and Dead-Letter Queues
Background processing introduces an important operational problem.
What happens if a worker receives a message but cannot process it?
For example, an email provider may be unavailable.
You should not simply discard the message.
Reliable messaging systems need mechanisms for retrying failed work and isolating messages that repeatedly fail.
A. What is a retry queue?
A retry queue temporarily holds messages that failed processing and need another attempt.
The email service returns a temporary error.
The worker can place the message into a retry mechanism rather than permanently losing it.
Immediate Retry: Try processing again immediately.
Exponential Backoff: Increase the delay after each failed attempt.
Retry Queue: Move the failed message to a separate queue and return it for processing later.
C. What is a Dead-Letter Queue?
A Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) stores messages that cannot be successfully processed under the configured delivery or retry policy.
A message has exceeded its retry limit.
A consumer repeatedly encounters an unrecoverable error.
Instead of retrying forever, the message can be moved to a DLQ for investigation.
Store failed messages for investigation and controlled redelivery
These are illustrative values. Different workloads need different retry schedules.
A poison message is a message that repeatedly causes processing to fail.
For example, a notification message contains an invalid date format.
If the worker retries it indefinitely, it may consume resources without ever succeeding.
RabbitMQ supports dead-letter exchanges and queues.
You will learn how to configure:
Why this lesson matters: A reliable messaging system must ensure that temporary failures can be retried while permanent failures are isolated rather than silently lost.
One important rule in distributed messaging is that you should not assume a message will always be delivered and processed exactly once.
A consumer may receive the same event more than once.
Your system must be prepared to handle this.
A. Why do duplicate events happen?
The broker does not know that the email operation succeeded.
The message may be delivered again after the consumer restarts.
The result could be two identical emails.
An idempotent consumer processes the same logical event without repeating its business effect.
For example, if an event has already been processed, the consumer can identify it and avoid performing the operation again.
Every event should have a unique identifier.
The consumer records processed event IDs.
A unique constraint can enforce that the same consumer does not record the same event twice.

@Transactional public void processEnrollmentEvent( EnrollmentEvent event) { if (processedEventRepository.existsByEventIdAndConsumerName( event.eventId(), "notification-service")) { return; } // Perform the business operation. processedEventRepository.save( new ProcessedEvent( event.eventId(), "notification-service" ) ); }
This illustrates the logic, but the exists check and insert should not be treated as a concurrency-safe guarantee by themselves.
For production, use a unique database constraint and an atomic insert-or-deduplicate strategy, with the event-processing record and the relevant business change committed together where possible.
At-most-once: A message is processed zero or one time. Duplicates are avoided, but messages may be lost.
At-least-once: A message is delivered one or more times. It is less likely to be lost, but duplicates are possible.
Exactly-once processing: A stronger guarantee about business effects. It requires careful coordination of message acknowledgement, state changes and external side effects.
For external operations such as email delivery, genuine exactly-once delivery is generally not guaranteed by the broker alone.
You will learn to design effectively-once business processing using idempotency and controlled side effects.
Why this lesson matters: Duplicate events are a normal possibility in distributed systems. Reliable consumers must prevent repeated business effects.
Building a background worker is relatively easy.
Building one that can handle crashes, retries, duplicate messages, scaling and service outages is much more challenging.
This lesson brings the previous concepts together.
A. What makes a background task reliable?
Execute independently of the main request.
Have a clearly defined input contract.
Provide a way to investigate permanently failed jobs.
A background job may move through several states:
For important background tasks, you may maintain a job record.
This is useful when the application needs to show users the state of long-running operations.
The job record and message queue serve different purposes:
The database tracks application job state.
The message broker transports and distributes work.
Suppose a worker crashes while processing a message.
Whether the broker will redeliver the message.
Whether the worker acknowledged it too early.
Whether the processing operation already completed.
Whether the next worker will detect duplicate execution.
Whether a job-processing lease or timeout is required.
Imagine 10,000 notifications arrive within a minute, but your email provider can process only 100 per minute.
Without backpressure, the system may overload workers or the provider.
Pause or throttle producers when required.
A common reliability problem occurs when the backend commits a database transaction but fails to publish its corresponding message.
The enrolment exists, but no notification message is published.
The Transactional Outbox Pattern addresses this by saving both the business record and the event record inside the same database transaction.
A separate publisher later sends pending events to the message broker.
This pattern builds directly on the partial-failure concepts covered in Module 06.
Why this lesson matters: Reliable background processing requires more than moving work out of an API request. It requires a complete execution, recovery and monitoring strategy.

sections.title: 4. Practical Lab — Build an Asynchronous Notification System with a Cache-Backed API

blocks.text: In this lab, you will build a notification system for a learning platform.
The system will accept notification requests, publish them to RabbitMQ, process them through background workers and cache frequently accessed course information using Redis.
PostgreSQL will remain the authoritative database for application records.
Automatic retry for temporary delivery failures.
Receives requests and applies business rules
Consumes messages, sends email and updates delivery status
D. Step 1 — Create the Database Entities
Use Redis to cache commonly accessed course data.
Retrieve course details from Redis when available.
Load from PostgreSQL on a cache miss.
Invalidate cache when course information changes.
Test the API with Redis enabled and disabled.
Measure the differences in response time and database query frequency under the same workload.
F. Step 3 — Implement the Enrolment Event
When a student successfully enrols in a course:
Save the StudentEnrolled event in the outbox.
Let the outbox publisher publish the event to RabbitMQ.
The original enrolment API should not wait for the email provider to finish sending the message.
G. Step 4 — Implement the Notification Producer
Create an event publisher that sends messages to RabbitMQ.

@Service public class NotificationPublisher { private final RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate; public NotificationPublisher( RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate) { this.rabbitTemplate = rabbitTemplate; } public void publish(EnrollmentEvent event) { rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend( "notification.exchange", "enrollment.confirmed", event ); } }
For the practical implementation, use the transactional outbox publisher rather than relying on a direct database-write-plus-message-publish sequence.
H. Step 5 — Implement the Notification Consumer
Create a background worker to process incoming events.
Maintain separate statuses where appropriate, such as:
Do not mark an email as successfully delivered merely because the notification record was created.
I. Step 6 — Implement Retry and Dead-Letter Handling
Move permanently failed messages to a DLQ.
Do not retry permanently invalid recipient data indefinitely.
Simulate the same enrolment event being delivered multiple times.
Every event must have a unique ID.
Avoid sending duplicate emails where the provider's capabilities allow idempotent submission.
Remember that an email provider may accept an email and then the worker may crash before recording success. Broker deduplication alone cannot guarantee that the recipient receives exactly one email.
Protect user-specific endpoints so that users can access only their own notifications.
API falls back to PostgreSQL where appropriate
Message/job can recover according to delivery configuration

sections.title: 5. Assignment — Implement Background Processing and Caching for a Course Platform

blocks.text: Build a backend system for an online learning platform where thousands of students access courses, enrol in programs and receive notifications.
Your application should improve API performance through caching and process time-consuming operations asynchronously.
Part A — Database and Application Design
Define the relevant relationships, indexes, constraints and status fields.
Create producers and consumers for these events.
Notifications must be processed independently of the main API request.
Implement at least three scheduled tasks:
Send learning reminders to inactive students.
Clean up expired notification or temporary records.
Demonstrate how you prevent the same scheduled task from running independently on every backend instance when only one global execution is intended.
Implement reliable cache invalidation after database updates.
Implement the transactional outbox pattern for at least one business event.
Demonstrate how the application recovers when the message broker or Redis becomes temporarily unavailable.
Compare API behaviour under different workloads:
Use the same workload for meaningful comparisons.

Your submission should include the architecture diagram, database schema, Java source code, Redis configuration, RabbitMQ configuration, producer and consumer implementations, notification worker, caching strategy, retry and DLQ configuration, scheduled tasks, outbox implementation, test cases and a performance report.
After completing the lab and assignment, you should be able to reason about the following situations.
Your enrolment API takes 15 seconds because it waits for email delivery. How will you move notification processing into the background without compromising enrolment consistency?
Redis becomes unavailable during peak traffic. How will your application continue serving course information without immediately overwhelming PostgreSQL?
An instructor updates a course, but thousands of users continue seeing old information. How will your cache invalidation system solve this?
A notification worker crashes after sending an email but before acknowledging the message. What happens when the broker redelivers it?
PostgreSQL successfully records an enrolment, but RabbitMQ is unavailable. How will you guarantee that the notification event is eventually published?
Your application receives 50,000 notification events, but your email provider has a much smaller processing capacity. How will you control queue growth and worker concurrency?
The same StudentEnrolled event reaches three notification workers. How will you make sure the business operation is performed only once?
Your backend runs on five servers, and a nightly report scheduler executes on all five. How will you ensure that only one intended global report-generation job runs?
A popular course's Redis key expires while 10,000 students request it simultaneously. How will you prevent all requests from querying PostgreSQL?
A malformed notification repeatedly fails processing. How will you isolate it without blocking other valid notifications?
These scenarios test whether you understand how caching and asynchronous systems behave under real production conditions.
Throughout this module, follow these principles:
Do not make users wait for work that can safely be processed independently.
Keep authoritative application data in an appropriate persistent database.
Use background workers for long-running operations.
Configure bounded thread pools and controlled concurrency.
Use message brokers for reliable work distribution.
Use Redis caching only where the data access pattern justifies it.
Give cached values appropriate expiration and invalidation policies.
Never assume database and cache writes are automatically atomic.
Acknowledge messages only after the required processing has succeeded.
Assume messages may be delivered more than once.
Use retries with limits and appropriate delays.
Isolate permanently failing messages using a DLQ.
Use an outbox pattern when database changes and event publication must remain coordinated.
Monitor queues, workers, caches and background jobs.
For deeper study, explore these official resources:
[Spring Scheduling and Asynchronous Execution](https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/integration/scheduling.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — background execution and scheduling.
[Apache Kafka Documentation](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — event streaming and consumer groups.
[Spring Data Redis Caching](https://docs.spring.io/spring-data/redis/reference/redis/redis-cache.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — Redis-backed caching with Spring.
By the end of Module 07, you should understand how professional backend applications improve performance and process work independently of user-facing requests.

You will know how to use Redis to reduce repeated database queries, RabbitMQ to distribute background tasks, event-driven architecture to connect independent components, and background workers to process notifications and other long-running operations.

You will also understand that asynchronous processing introduces new engineering challenges, including duplicate events, message delivery failures, queue backlogs, cache inconsistency and worker crashes.
Background jobs handle independent and long-running work.
Message brokers distribute tasks between components.
Redis improves frequently accessed data retrieval.
Cache invalidation keeps cached information reasonably fresh.
Retry queues recover from temporary failures.
Dead-letter queues isolate permanently failing messages.
Idempotent consumers prevent duplicate business effects.
Transactional outbox patterns coordinate database changes and event publication.

Your final objective: Be able to design and implement a high-performance backend that combines Redis caching, asynchronous task execution, message queues and reliable event processing to support a growing real-world platform such as PrepSpaces.
